content: The Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine has been shown to be effective in reducing the risk of leprosy, with evidence indicating a 55% reduction in risk when administered at birth. However, the degree of protection varies across studies, most of which were conducted in countries with a high burden of leprosy. The vaccine is widely available and already included in the vaccination policies of most leprosy-endemic countries. In addition to BCG, other vaccines using killed mycobacteria have demonstrated similar or slightly lower efficacy in preventing leprosy. Among these, only the Mycobacterium indicum pranii (formerly M. w) vaccine is currently in production. Two large randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on BCG revaccination yielded conflicting results: one showed no significant difference in leprosy rates between groups, while the other reported a 49% reduction in risk with revaccination compared to placebo. Consequently, the effectiveness of BCG revaccination remains uncertain. Data from the COLEP SDR trial suggest that BCG at birth may enhance the protective effect of single-dose rifampicin (SDR) chemoprophylaxis in contacts of leprosy patients. An ongoing RCT is investigating the impact of BCG revaccination in a large cohort of leprosy contacts. The WHO Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) has concluded that BCG vaccination at birth is effective in reducing leprosy risk and should be maintained, particularly in high-burden settings. Evidence also suggests that BCG at birth may increase the protective effect of SDR in contacts from 57% to 80%, although this evidence is of low quality. The effectiveness of a second dose of BCG (revaccination) remains unclear due to conflicting trial results. Moderate-quality evidence supports the efficacy of the M. indicum pranii vaccine in preventing leprosy. In February 2018, the WHO released a revised policy on BCG use for the prevention of both tuberculosis (TB) and leprosy, summarizing these findings. WHO staff will provide direct support to country program officers adapting the guidelines. Regional workshops for guideline adaptation may be organized if resources allow. The GLP will also work with the International Federation of Anti-Leprosy Associations (ILEP) to disseminate the guidelines through its technical commission and network of country coordinators. The WHO Steering Group will evaluate the accessibility and acceptability of the guidelines during the first year of implementation. Metrics such as the number of downloads from WHO websites and requests for hard copies will be monitored. Post-implementation, the impact of the guidelines will be assessed through epidemiological data reviews, uptake of recommendations, and identification of barriers to effective implementation. The WHO will also monitor the impact of the guidelines on health outcomes, including treatment compliance and disease trends among leprosy contacts. Data on preventive treatment with SDR will be collected through the annual leprosy data collection tool, in use since 2016. The guidelines are expected to remain valid until at least 2022 unless significant new evidence necessitates an earlier review. Research priorities include the evaluation of diagnostic tools, such as PCR tests and imaging techniques, and the development of new biomarkers for leprosy detection. Longitudinal studies are needed to assess the predictive value of these tools for leprosy development in contacts. Research on treatment strategies for drug-resistant leprosy is also critical, with observational studies recommended to evaluate the outcomes of alternative regimens. Trials on new and existing vaccines, including the LepVax subunit vaccine, are needed to explore their potential in leprosy prevention. The WHO recommends evaluating new TB vaccines for their potential to prevent other mycobacterial diseases, such as leprosy and Buruli ulcer.
